title: You didn’t notice it at first.
paragraphs: You didn’t notice it at first.
The music was loud. The celebration was holy. The presence of God was returning to the city.
“As the ark of the Lord came into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart.”
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
The Real Issue Was the Heart
“David danced before the Lord with all his might.” — 2 Samuel 6:14

No image to protect.
No reputation to maintain.
No pride left to defend.

But Michal?
She watched from a distance.
Worship from a distance always turns into judgment.
Spiritual Diagnosis: Pride Masked as Dignity

Michal wasn’t just any woman.
She was royalty. The daughter of Saul.
She grew up around image, control, and appearances.

David?
He stripped that away in one moment of radical humility.
“I will make myself yet more contemptible than this… and I will be abased in your eyes.” — 2 Samuel 6:22
David chose humility before God over honor before people.
Identity Mirror: This Is Closer Than You Think

Someone worships freely.
Hands raised. Tears falling. No shame.

That subtle resistance?
That quiet discomfort?
The Hidden Wound Behind Michal’s Contempt
She was once given to David, then taken away, then returned like property (see 1 Samuel 25:44, 2 Samuel 3:13–16).
And instead of healing before God…
Because unresolved pain often turns into criticism of those who are free.

David was free.
Michal was bound.
And freedom will always offend bondage.
The Turning Point: Worship Reveals Allegiance
“It was before the Lord… who chose me above your father…” — 2 Samuel 6:21

Michal saw a man.
David saw a throne.

Michal saw embarrassment.
David saw glory.
The chapter ends with something chilling:
“And Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.” — 2 Samuel 6:23
Spiritual barrenness often follows a heart that despises true worship.
You reject the very thing God uses to bring life.
But there is a greater King — Jesus Christ — who did something far more “undignified.”

He was stripped.
Mocked.
Crucified publicly.
“He humbled himself by becoming obedient to death—even death on a cross.” — Philippians 2:8

For your pride.
For your resistance.
For your cold, distant heart.

Observe… or surrender.
Judge… or repent.
Stay guarded… or be broken before God.
Because true worship will cost you your image.
But it will give you your soul.
You don’t struggle with worship style.
